title: One scene in three hand-painted styles
creator: higgsfield_ai
prompt:
# Style tests — 8 × 10 s, pure 2D code

Goal: the SAME 10-second mini-scene drawn in 8 different illustration/animation styles, so the client can pick a look for

"The Cloud Shepherd" (a wordless short about a girl and a small cloud spirit). Each test must look like it was entirely

hand-made in that style — painted/drawn, never 3D-rendered, never "vector clip-art". Quality bar: a festival-grade style frame

that moves. Original characters only — no existing film/series characters, logos or famous artworks copied.

## The scene (identical beats in every style, 10.0 s, 1920×1080, 24 fps)

1. 0.0–3.5 s  WIDE: a grassy hill under a big sky, one lone tree on top, wind moving grass/leaves/clouds. A small figure

   (the girl) runs up the slope from the lower left toward the tree.

2. 3.5–6.5 s  MEDIUM: the girl (≈7 y.o., black bob hair, straw hat with a red ribbon, light-blue dress, white collar)

   arrives at the tree, catches her breath, holds her hat in the wind, looks around.

3. 6.5–10.0 s CLOSE-ish two-shot: a tiny white cloud spirit (round puffy body, two dot eyes, pink blush, no mouth or a tiny one)

   peeks from behind the trunk; she sees it, her face lights up; it floats out shyly and settles on the brim of her hat; she laughs.

Hard cuts between the three shots. Camera: locked or a slow smooth drift — no shake, no fast zooms. Characters can animate on

twos (12 fps poses) where that suits the style; wind/clouds smooth.

Interpret the characters FULLY in the style (proportions, line, colour, shapes, pattern) — they must stay recognisable

(bob hair, straw hat w/ red ribbon, blue dress; white puffy cloud spirit) but redesigned for the style.

## Tech

- Your folder: `~/Claude/motion-studio/films/style-tests/<slug>/` with `index.html` + any js modules. Canvas2D (or SVG) only.

  No three.js / WebGL 3D. Offscreen canvases for heavy static paintings (paint once in setup, reuse).

- Contract for the renderer (headless Chrome): the page must define

  `window.HF = { meta: { w: 1920, h: 1080, fps: 24, duration: 10 }, isReady: false, seek: async (t) => { drawFrame(t) } }`

  and set `HF.isReady = true` when ready. Every frame is a PURE function of t (seeded rng, never Math.random/Date/rAF).

- Stills: `cd ~/Claude/motion-studio && node engine/render.mjs films/style-tests/<slug>/index.html --stills 1,4.5,8,9.5 --outdir /tmp/st_<slug>`

  Look at them (Read the PNGs) and iterate until it really looks like the style — at least 3 rounds of self-critique against

  what a real artist of that style would draw.

- Final: `node engine/render.mjs films/style-tests/<slug>/index.html --mb 1 --workers 4 --crf 16 --out films/style-tests/<slug>/<slug>.mp4`

- Frame cost < 200 ms. Fonts: none needed (no on-screen text — the lead adds labels).

- Shared helpers you MAY copy from (not required): `~/Claude/motion-studio/films/cloud-shepherd-2d/lib/paint.js` (watercolor wash,

  pencil strokes, grass field, crowns, cumulus), `lib/time.js` (easing, rng, noise). Don't edit files outside your folder.

## Report back (short)

Path to the mp4, 3–5 lines on the style decisions (palette, line, texture, motion), and what is still weak.

title: Drum'n'bass violin hyperflip music video
creator: grmchn4ai
prompt:
# 作曲依頼：制御された狂気を持つドラムンベース

とびきりクレイジーで、音楽的にも最高に気持ちのいいドラムンベースとそのMVを作ってほしい。

ベースになるのはDrill 'n' Bassのような、激しく複雑で予測不能なドラムパターン。目まぐるしく変化するブレイクビーツ、細かなリズムの切り刻み、意表を突くフィルなどを大量に盛り込んでほしい。ただし、単にランダムで騒々しいだけの音楽にはしたくない。どれだけ狂ったリズムでも、全体として強烈なグルーヴがあって、思わず身体が動いてしまうような音楽にしてほしい。

そこに、バイオリンを中心とした弦楽器の音色を大胆に組み合わせてほしい。弦楽器ならではの生々しい響きや感情的なフレーズと、激しい電子ダンスミュージックが融合している感じが理想。単にストリングスを背景に敷くだけではなく、楽曲の主役としても活躍させたい。

一方で、クラブミュージックらしい、非常にモダンでキラキラしたシンセサウンドもたっぷり使ってほしい。透明感のある美しい電子音から、鋭く派手で未来的な音色まで、アコースティックな弦楽器とは対照的なデジタルサウンドを生かして、音色の面でも驚かせてほしい。

特にこだわりたいのが曲の展開。ドロップの後やブリッジなどでは、HyperflipやComplextroのように、ごく短い区間で次々と異なる音色やフレーズ、リズムが切り替わっていくような、超高密度で複雑な展開を取り入れてほしい。まるで短い音楽的アイデアが猛烈な勢いで入れ替わり、互いに掛け合っているような感じ。ただし、これも単なる音の寄せ集めではなく、一連の音楽として成立させてほしい。

全体として、強烈なリズム、美しい弦楽器、きらびやかな電子音、そして予想を裏切る複雑な展開が共存する作品にしたい。

ジャンルの定型に収まる必要はないし、むしろ積極的に実験してほしい。でも、実験的だからといって音楽としての気持ちよさを犠牲にはしないでほしい。

**聴いていて「何だこれは！」と驚くのに、なぜか最高に気持ちよくて、何度も聴きたくなる。そんな一曲を期待している。**

If an input is missing, use the sourcing rules in phase 2. Never invent a fact, number,
date, quote or customer. A claim appears on screen only if the founder says it on camera
or I gave you a source.

## 1. Understand the footage before writing anything

1. List every clip with its length, resolution and frame rate (ffprobe).
2. Transcribe every clip with word-level timestamps (faster-whisper or similar).
   Save one JSON per clip: each word with start and end time.
3. Fix the transcript's spelling of names and brand terms by hand. Speech models
   misspell them. Keep the timings.
4. Read the transcripts and mark the strongest lines:
   - the hook: the single most surprising thing the founder says about themselves
   - who they are (name and title, in their own words)
   - the proof: what they built before, in their words
   - the theme: the idea that connects past work to this company
   - the turn: the line where they name the new company
   - a closing line with personality
5. Show me the picked lines with clip and timestamps. Checkpoint 1.

## 2. Source what's missing

Real footage first, generated footage only to fill gaps, and say which is which.

A. Founder interview. If there's none, ask me to record one. Give me a shot brief:
   seated, eye level, 1080p or better, natural light, 5 questions that produce the six
   line types above. Do not fake the founder speaking.

B. Archive b-roll for history and context (gives the documentary feel).
   - Internet Archive, Prelinger collection: old industrial and educational films.
     Use only items whose license field says public domain. Check each item's
     license URL yourself, don't assume.
   - Library of Congress, NASA, US government film: public domain, still check.
   - Skip anything non-commercial-only, anything with a recognisable brand, and
     any live music archive.
   - Pick 6 to 10 short shots (3 to 6 seconds each) that picture the eras or ideas
     in the founder's story. Trim them, keep the source title and year for an
     on-screen credit.

C. Owned event or press footage (a launch, a stage moment, an exchange listing).
   Use it under the line where the founder mentions that moment. Keep its real
   audio if it has a distinctive sound (applause, a bell) for the sound design.

D. Period music. For a story half that looks back, use a public-domain recording:
   a pre-1926 78rpm transfer from the Internet Archive's 78 collection works well
   (solo piano is the safest bed under speech). Confirm the recording date.

E. AI-generated footage, only for shots with no people speaking:
   - An opening "walk-in": the empty interview location, then the founder walks in
     and sits. Make it with an image-to-video model that accepts a start frame and
     an end frame. Start frame = the interview's first frame with the person removed
     (image edit model). End frame = the real first frame of the interview. The
     generated clip then cuts invisibly into the real footage. Compare the last
     generated frame with the real frame and regenerate if they differ visibly.
   - Some video models refuse real people's likenesses. If one refuses, try another
     that allows a supplied end frame. Only do this for a person who has agreed.
   - Never generate the founder's voice or put words in their mouth.

F. Narrator voice. Generate with a text-to-speech model (a local open model is
   fine). One consistent voice for every narrator line. After generating each line,
   transcribe it and compare against the script word for word. Regenerate until it
   matches. Check numbers, prices and the brand name especially. Trim silence, but
   use a gentle threshold at the start so a soft first word isn't cut.

G. Faces and avatars in diagrams. Use generated or illustrated faces, never real
   people who haven't agreed.

Show me a list of every asset, where it came from and its license. Checkpoint 2.

## 3. Write the story

Structure (adjust lengths to the lines you have):

| Beat | Length | Voice | Picture |
|---|---|---|---|
| Open | 6 to 9 s | Narrator, 2 short lines that set a theme without giving away the hook | Walk-in or a slow establishing shot, cinematic bars |
| Who | 3 to 4 s | Founder says name and title | Full frame, then shrinks to a card beside a name plate |
| Hook | 4 to 5 s | Founder's most surprising claim | Words slam in over full-frame footage, then a designed reveal |
| Proof | 3 to 4 s | Founder on what it became | Owned event footage, one stat or stamp in their words |
| Bridge | 3 to 4 s | Narrator, one line on the bigger pattern | Full-screen archive montage, hard cuts, year labels |
| How it worked | 6 to 8 s | Founder | A diagram that builds as the nouns are spoken |
| Theme | 5 to 7 s | Founder | A three-step timeline: past, their earlier work, today |
| Turn | 4 to 5 s | Founder names the company | Back to full frame, then a logo moment |
| Product | 7 to 8 s | Narrator, 2 lines | Product UI and one concrete benefit |
| Belief | 4 s | Founder | Card plus one simple graphic of the idea |
| Close | 3 s | Founder, a line with personality | Full frame, one small product touch |
| End card | 4 s | none | Headline, tagline, URL, logo |

Rules:
- The narrator must speak in the first 10 seconds and again around 20 seconds, so
  viewers know the film has two voices before the narrator explains the product.
- Narrator lines are short: 6 to 12 words each. The founder carries the story.
- Reorder the founder's lines freely, but never cut inside a sentence in a way
  that changes its meaning.
- Write the narrator lines and all on-screen text. Follow my terms list.
- Show me the script as a table: time, who speaks, exact words, what's on screen.
  Checkpoint 3.

## 4. Cut the audio and build the timeline

1. Cut each founder line from the source by timestamp, video and audio separately.
   Leave about 0.06 s before the first word.
2. TRAP: word end times from the transcript are often early. After cutting, transcribe
   each cut clip on its own and confirm the last word is whole. Years and numbers at
   the end of a line get clipped most. Extend the cut until it reads correctly.
3. Clean the founder audio lightly: high-pass around 90 Hz, mild noise reduction,
   gentle compression, and normalise every voice clip to the same loudness
   (about -19 LUFS) so founder and narrator sit level.
4. Write a script that lays the lines end to end with small gaps and saves a timeline
   file: start time of every line, plus the time of every key word that a graphic
   should hit ("the year", "public", "customers", the company name).
   The picture and the music both read this one file, so they can't drift.

## 5. Design and animate

Build it as code so every frame is repeatable: Remotion (React), or HTML with a
paused GSAP timeline rendered frame by frame through a headless browser. 1920x1080,
30 fps. Put the composition in its own entry file.

The core device: the founder's video lives in ONE card that moves through the film.
- Define its rectangle (x, y, width, height, corner radius) as keyframes on the
  timeline and ease between them over about 0.4 s.
- Start each move exactly on a cut between two interview lines. The move hides the
  jump cut, and the founder stays on screen while graphics build beside them.
- Full frame for the emotional lines (who, hook start, the turn, the close).
  Card for the explaining lines.
- In card mode give it corner brackets, a thin accent outline, a soft shadow and a
  small name tag with a recording dot. Fade those out as it returns to full frame.

The world behind the cards: dark brand background, a slow drifting accent glow, a
faint perspective grid scrolling toward the viewer, sparse floating particles, light
film grain over everything. It should look like one designed space, not slides.

Scene recipes (reuse and adapt):
- Word slam: the founder's exact words appear one at a time, each landing on the
  frame the word is spoken, large, with one phrase in the accent color.
- Year rollback: a huge serif number counts down from this year to the year in the
  story and lands on the spoken word, with a period-correct interface beside it
  (an old operating system window typing a first message, for example).
- Name plate: serif name rising from a mask, a rule drawing across, title rows
  arriving as each title is spoken.
- Proof card: owned footage in a tilted rounded card, a stamp that slaps on at the
  key word, a line chart drawing itself with NO axis numbers unless sourced.
- Archive montage: full-bleed archive film, black and white with a slight sepia,
  flicker, vignette, slow push-in, hard cuts, big serif year and a mono label,
  a small source credit, a three-segment progress marker.
- Building diagram: three columns of nodes that appear as each noun is spoken,
  lines drawing between them with dots travelling along, and one column flipping
  to a new state on the key word.
- Timeline: three cards (archive clip, the founder's earlier product, today's
  product UI) with a line connecting them on the word that names the connection,
  plus two pills for the two ideas being joined.
- Turn: a progress line from the old company to the new one over full-frame footage,
  then a two-color wipe into the logo on a dark field.
- Product: a checklist ticking itself off beside a tilted UI card and a notification.
- End card: headline in two lines rising from masks, tagline in serif italic,
  URL in a pill that pulses once, logo.

Captions: word-by-word captions for every spoken line, bottom center, in a dark
pill, current word in the accent color, at most 7 words on screen. Hide them only
when the same words are already on screen as a word slam.

Craft rules:
- One focal element per moment. Three type sizes, two weights. One spacing scale.
- Sans for labels and UI, serif for names, years and the brand's voice.
- Nothing moves without a cause. Every graphic lands on a spoken word.
- A small 3 percent push-in on the whole frame at every cut.
- Brand colors only. Accent color is for emphasis, not decoration.

## 6. Music and sound

Write the score as a script that reads the timeline file.

- Story half: the public-domain period recording, faded in over 1.5 s.
- At the moment the founder names the company, tape-stop the recording (playback
  rate falls to zero over about 0.75 s).
- From the logo on: a simple modern bed you synthesise (kick, soft bass, a plucked
  pattern, hats) at around 100 to 105 BPM, starting with one low hit.
- Duck all music by about 8 dB under every spoken line, with a slow release.

Sound design, physical sounds only:
- a soft low thump when the card lands in a new position
- a projector rattle under archive film
- quiet mechanical taps for counters and diagram nodes
- real audio from owned footage where it has character
- NO synthetic whooshes, risers, laser sweeps or chimes. They make it sound cheap.

Master to -14 LUFS with true peak under -1 dB. Apply gain and a limiter, not a
dynamic normaliser, so the balance you set survives.

## 7. Check before you show me

1. Render still frames every 2 seconds into one contact sheet and look at it.
   Fix: black or frozen video (a clip shorter than its slot), text over a face,
   anything clipped at an edge, a graphic that arrives before or after its word.
2. Transcribe the finished mix and compare with the script. Every line must come
   through. Brand-name spelling differences are fine.
3. Measure loudness and peak.
4. Check every on-screen claim against the founder's words or my sources.
5. Check every term against my avoid list.
6. Tell me plainly what you could not verify. You cannot hear the mix, so say so
   and name the two things I should listen for.

## 8. Deliver

- Master MP4 (1080p, H.264, AAC), plus a small 720p preview.
- A scene table: time, who speaks, what's on screen.
- The asset list with sources and licenses, and which shots are AI-generated.
- The build scripts, so a change request is a re-render, not a rebuild.

## Revision habits

- If I say the open is too fast, restore the slow establishing open and move the
  hook to just after the founder's name.
- If I say a voice appears from nowhere, give that voice a line in the first
  10 seconds.
- If I say it feels like a slideshow, add full-screen real footage earlier and
  keep the founder on screen in the card.
- If I say the sound is synthetic, remove effects before adding any.

title: Animal pilots battle a golden orrery
creator: anstapnever
prompt:
Create a 2D anime short. It must look completely like real Japanese anime, as if it were taken directly from a finished theatrical anime film. This is traditional-looking, hand-drawn 2D anime, not a 3D animation, a moving illustration, or a stylized web graphic.

Build everything in three.js (WebGL2) in the browser, render every frame headless in Chrome with a painted-background brush pass and an ink pass, and encode with ffmpeg. Deliver one 1920x1080, 24 fps MP4 with an orchestral soundtrack. Use any tools, libraries, references, guides, literally anything, as long as the final result looks 100% like hand-drawn 2D anime.

REFERENCE
Retell Operation Yashima from Neon Genesis Evangelion shot for shot: the same actions, staging, camera angles, lens feel and timing. Redesign every visual from scratch, so the scene is recognisable only by what happens, never by how anything looks. 79.4 seconds, 34 shots.

HOOK
In the first 3 seconds something must already be happening. Frame 0: darkness is eating a glowing city block by block. No fade in. A gold pulse races along the power lines into a mountain-sized gun. A ring in the sky turns and looks at the camera.

WORLD
A harbour country at night under a huge moon and teal aurora: terraced towns of ochre houses with thousands of lit windows, stone seawalls, power pylons over snowy conifer hills, basalt cliffs, a ridge with a giant rail cannon built from transformers and truss. Ground, rock and walls show structure at three scales: blotches, cracks, chips.

CHARACTERS
The pilots are anthropomorphic animals with big anime eyes: an otter boy with brass goggles and a calm snow-leopard girl. Technicians are raccoons and badgers. The enemy is the Orrery, a floating golden astrolabe of nested rings around a ruby core. The machines are the Heron, a white and red sniper mech, and the Tortoise, a squat copper and dark teal mech with a ship's-bow shield.

STORY
The power of a whole country goes out, block by block, and flows into one gun. The Orrery fires back and the two beams twist around each other and both miss. While the gun recharges, the Orrery fires again and the Tortoise jumps in front of it, holding a shield that melts away in the beam. The second shot pierces the core, and the Orrery falls apart in silence. The boy tears open the burning hatch with bare paws. She opens her eyes, and for the first time she smiles. The lights come back across the country, and in one small round window a lamp comes on.

LIGHT
Deep saturated night, never murky: ultramarine, teal, gold. Every beam and blast lights the land and machines near it, and light only changes with a visible cause. Cel light with hard shadows, gouache backgrounds, ink lines on every character and machine, and fire as inked billows.

MOTION
Living things shift weight, plant their feet without sliding, anticipate, overshoot and settle, with follow-through on ears, tails and clothes. Heavy machines land with mass. Characters on twos, FX on threes.

SOUND
Real orchestral samples (CC0), mood decided second by second, in C minor until the very last beat: wires humming in the hook, dread, a tutti on the first shot, a held breath before the shield hit, near-total silence as the enemy falls, a single flute at the hatch, and the only major chord of the film when the lamp comes back on.

TEAM
Parallel agent departments, each owning its own files: world, enemy, machines, characters, FX, sound. A shared map and shot list keep them in sync.

CHECKS
Before the final render a script tests the frames on the real geometry with BVH: no hand or foot inside the armour, the ground or another body; the camera never enters a mesh or goes below ground; no camera jerks; nothing appears or vanishes in the middle of a shot.

title: Steam locomotive transforms into robot
creator: 0kncn
prompt:
Create a 2D anime short. It must look completely like real Japanese anime, as if it were taken directly from a finished theatrical anime film. This is traditional-looking, hand-drawn 2D anime, not a 3D animation, a moving illustration, or a stylized web graphic.

Build everything in Blender from Python, render it in Eevee, then ink and paint every frame in a second pass. Deliver one 1920x1080, 24 fps MP4 with a synthesized soundtrack. Use any tools, libraries, references, guides, literally anything, as long as the final result looks 100% like hand-drawn 2D anime.

Use theatrical anime as the art style reference for the design, line work, painted backgrounds, color and atmosphere. The film is 90 seconds long (2160 frames), in 42 shots. Its hero is a steam locomotive that transforms into a robot. No people appear in the film.

HERO
No. 9, a 1940s 2-8-2 freight locomotive with a four-axle tender, 23 m long, asleep for decades in a mountain engine shed: matte black boiler with rust runs, faded red wheel centres and buffer beam, brass number plate "9", one large headlamp, two amber marker lamps, moss on the running boards, ivy through the cab windows, and a stork's nest on the cab roof. As a robot it stands 21 m tall with its shoulders at 17 m. It is an original design, not a character from any existing series. It moves on twos, slow and heavy. Its wheels never slip and its feet never slide.

TRANSFORM
One transformation, at full speed, 120 frames, in five stages of 24 frames. Every part is rigid: nothing stretches, nothing vanishes, nothing appears. Each part travels on a hinge or a slide you can see.
1. Legs: the tender uncouples, splits lengthwise and swings down; its two bogies lock as feet, the coal stays in bunkers on the calves.
2. Hips: the cab drops and widens into the pelvis; the trailing truck folds onto the lower back.
3. Torso: the boiler tilts upright, firebox at the waist, smokebox at the top; the chimney and steam dome end on the upper back and keep venting.
4. Arms: the running boards swing out with the cylinders as shoulders, the piston and connecting rods as forearms, and hands with three fingers and a thumb unfolding from the valve gear; the front driving wheels ride up as shoulder discs, the rear ones fold to hips and knees.
5. Head: the smokebox door hinges forward as the chest plate with the headlamp at its centre; a riveted helmet rises from the smokebox with one dark visor slit and the two marker lamps as amber eyes; the cowcatcher folds up as a collar.
The cab roof panel rides up to the right shoulder and carries the stork's nest, never tilted more than 10 degrees.
Stages 1-3 happen on the rails, with the first strides landing on the ballast either side of the track. Stages 4-5 happen in the air.

WORLD
A single-track mountain railway at real scale. At the top, an ore mine with a loading bunker and a rake of twelve four-wheel hopper wagons. The line descends through larch forest and a short rock tunnel to a viaduct: seven 18 m steel girder spans on stone piers, 126 m long, the deck 17 m above a turquoise meltwater river 3 m deep. Beyond it, a small station: a stone engine shed, a water tower, a semaphore signal with an alarm bell, a signal box, a siding ending in a sand drag. Snow peaks behind, a cliff face above the viaduct, telegraph poles along the whole line.

STORY
A clear spring morning in the valley. Meltwater loosens the cliff: a rockfall hits the middle pier of the viaduct, the pier collapses into the river and the two girders it carried sag into a V, held only by the rails. Up at the mine the shock snaps a coupling and the twelve loaded wagons start to roll downhill, unmanned. At the station the semaphore drops to danger and the bell rings. In the dark shed the firebox glows, the pressure needle climbs, the headlamp lights; the stork flies up. No. 9 bursts through the shed doors tearing ivy and rust, and charges up the grade with the wagons coming down the other side. On the approach it transforms at full speed, leaps from the abutment, lands crouched in the river, wades to the fallen pier, and lifts the sagging joint onto its shoulders and raised hands. The wagons hit the viaduct: it sinks 0.3 m as each one passes over and holds. The rake runs through the station into the sand drag and stops. No. 9 does not come back out. It locks its knees and stays as the new pier. The steam thins, the stork returns to its nest, the visor dims.

LIGHT
High-key anime light, never murky: a morning sun from the south-east, a saturated cobalt sky, white cumulus with lavender shadows, snow peaks with blue shadows, fresh green larch, a turquoise river with drawn white water. Light only changes with a cause you can see: rock dust dims the gorge for 3 seconds, steam whites out a frame, the firebox throws orange onto the shed walls. Cel light with hard shadows, gouache backgrounds, ink lines on every machine, rail and building, effects drawn on twos: steam as inked rolling shapes with a flat shadow tone, water as inked sheets with foam crowns, dust as drawn clouds, never particle mush.

SOUND
A synthesized orchestra on a 144 bpm grid: one beat is 10 frames, and every cut lands on a multiple of 5 frames. A hopeful theme on clarinet and horn, the collapse in E minor, a 12/8 chase with the exhaust chuff as percussion at four beats per wheel revolution, a heavy 3/4 for the hold with one low drum per wagon. 16 hits land exactly on the picture: the rockfall, the pier, the coupling, the signal arm, the shed doors, each transformation lock, the landing, the lift, the first and last wagon. The steam whistle is heard twice: once on waking, once on the hold.

FORMAT
Write the film as a Python story clock: one state per frame for every pose, camera, wheel angle, rod position, transformation part, wagon, effect and sound cue.

CHECKS
Before the final render a script tests every frame on the real meshes: no part of No. 9 goes through another part, in either form or at any frame of the transformation; the total volume of its parts is the same in both forms; every wheel on a rail turns exactly as far as it travels; planted feet do not move; No. 9 never goes through the track, the shed, the viaduct or the riverbed; the wagons stay on the rails and never touch each other except at the couplings; the camera never enters a mesh, the cliff or the water; nothing jumps between frames.
